summary: This document describes the Diameter application used for authentication, authorization, and accounting in the Network Access Server environment. It obsoletes RFC 4005 and is used together with the Diameter Base protocol, Transport Profile, and EAP specifications.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC says how a device that gives people access to a network asks a central server three questions: is this person who they say they are, what may they do, and how much did they use. It defines the messages for that exchange and the fields they carry.

subtitle: How a network access server asks a Diameter server who may connect, what they may do, and what they used.

tldr.problem: A dial-up or broadband access server has to check who is calling, decide what the caller is allowed to do, and record what the caller used. Doing that with RADIUS works, but the message set is limited and hard to extend.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines the Diameter application used in the Network Access Server environment. It names the ten commands used for the exchange, lists the attributes that carry the call details, the credentials and the accounting figures, and gives the rules for when each attribute must or may appear.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7155 is a Standards Track document from April 2014 that obsoletes RFC 4005 and is not backward compatible with it. Together with the Diameter base protocol, its transport profile and the Extensible Authentication Protocol, it satisfies the network access requirements of RFC 2989 and RFC 3169.

today: RFC 7155 is a Standards Track document published in April 2014. It obsoletes RFC 4005 and is not backward compatible with it, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
This document describes the Diameter protocol application used for Authentication, Authorization and Accounting in the Network Access Server (NAS) environment. When combined with the Diameter Base protocol, RFC 6733, the Transport Profile of RFC 3539, and the Extensible Authentication Protocol specification of RFC 4072, this application specification satisfies the NAS-related requirements defined in RFC 2989 and RFC 3169.

The document first describes the operation of the application, then defines the Diameter message command codes, and then lists the attributes used in those messages, grouped by common usage: session identification, authentication, authorization, tunnelling and accounting. The authorization attributes are further broken down by service type.

The terminology of the Diameter Base protocol applies, with a few additions. A NAS is a device that provides an access service for a user to a network, and the service may be a network connection or a value-added service such as terminal emulation. PPP is a multiprotocol serial datalink and the primary IP datalink used for dial-in NAS connection service. CHAP is an authentication process used in PPP, while PAP is a deprecated PPP authentication process that is often still used for backward compatibility. SLIP is a serial datalink that only supports IP, a design prior to PPP. L2TP provides a dynamic mechanism for tunnelling Layer 2 circuits across a packet-oriented data network, and the L2TP Access Concentrator is the endpoint used to cross-connect an L2TP session directly to a datalink. LCP is one of the three major components of PPP, used to agree encapsulation options, handle limits on packet size, detect a looped-back link and terminate the link. PPTP allows PPP to be tunnelled through an IP network, and in this document the term VPN is used to describe access services that use tunnelling methods.

Two further points apply to every implementation. A Diameter node conforming to this specification MUST advertise its support by including the value 1 in the Auth-Application-Id of the Capabilities-Exchange-Request message, and the Auth-Application-Id AVP MUST be set to the value 1 in the AA-Request, Re-Auth-Request, Session-Termination-Request and Abort-Session-Request messages.
sections.plainLanguage: The access server is the box a caller connects to. This document defines the conversation between that box and a central server, and it also fixes the application number that both ends put in every message, so that each side knows which kind of exchange it is taking part in.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 4005
sections.content:
This document obsoletes RFC 4005 and is not backward compatible with it. An overview of the major changes is given in the RFC.

All of the material regarding RADIUS and Diameter protocol interactions has been removed, though where attributes are derived from RADIUS attributes, the range and format of those attribute values have been retained for ease of transition. The lists of RADIUS attribute values have been deleted in favour of references to the appropriate IANA registries.

The Command Code Format for the Accounting-Request and Accounting-Answer messages has been changed to explicitly require the inclusion of the Acct-Application-Id attribute and exclude the Vendor-Specific-Application-Id attribute. Normally such a change would require a new command code and a new application id, but the earlier document also required an instance of the Acct-Application-Id to be present, with the alternative being a Vendor-Specific-Application-Id grouped attribute that contained one. The syntax of the commands has therefore changed while the semantics have not, with the caveat that the Acct-Application-Id can no longer be nested inside the Vendor-Specific-Application-Id.

The accounting model to be used is now specified: it is RECOMMENDED that the coupled accounting model of RFC 6733 be used with this application, and the value of the Acct-Application-Id in the Accounting-Request and Accounting-Answer messages SHOULD be set to 1. There are many other miscellaneous fixes, such as corrected example IP addresses and clarifying references, and the errata reports filed against RFC 4005 at the time of writing have been reviewed and incorporated as necessary.
sections.plainLanguage: The earlier version mixed in material about how RADIUS and Diameter interact, and that has gone. The accounting messages were also reworded so that they name the accounting application directly rather than through a wrapper, which changes the bytes on the wire but not the meaning.

sections.title: Calls, Ports and Sessions
sections.content:
The arrival of a new call or service connection at a port of a Network Access Server starts a Diameter NAS Application message exchange. Information about the call, the identity of the user and the user's authentication information are packaged into a Diameter AA-Request message and sent to a server. The server processes the information and responds with a Diameter AA-Answer message that contains authorization information for the NAS or a failure code. The value DIAMETER_MULTI_ROUND_AUTH indicates an additional authentication exchange, and several request and answer messages may be exchanged until the transaction completes.

When the authentication or authorization exchange completes successfully, the NAS application SHOULD start a session context. If the Result-Code of DIAMETER_MULTI_ROUND_AUTH is returned, the exchange continues until a success or error is returned. If accounting is active, the application MUST also send an Accounting message, and an Accounting-Record-Type of START_RECORD is sent for a new session. If a session fails to start, the EVENT_RECORD message is sent with the reason for the failure described. The return of an unsupportable Accounting-Realtime-Required value would result in a failure to establish the session.

The Diameter Base protocol allows users to be periodically reauthenticated and reauthorized. The Session-Id in the request MUST be the same as the one present in the original authentication or authorization message. A Diameter server informs the NAS of the maximum time allowed before reauthentication or reauthorization through the Authorization-Lifetime attribute. A NAS MAY reauthenticate before the end of that period but MUST do so at the end of it, and the failure of a reauthentication exchange will terminate the service. A Diameter server may also issue an unsolicited Re-Auth-Request to the NAS, and the NAS MUST respond with a Re-Auth-Answer. If the request properly identifies an active session, the NAS initiates a new local reauthentication or authorization sequence as indicated by the Re-Auth-Request-Type value, causing a new AA-Request to be sent using the existing Session-Id, and the server answers with a new set of service parameters.

If accounting is active, every change of authentication or authorization SHOULD generate an accounting message. If the service is a continuation of the prior user context, an Accounting-Record-Type of INTERIM_RECORD indicating the new session attributes and cumulative status is appropriate. If a new user or a significant change in authorization is detected, the service may send two messages, STOP_RECORD and START_RECORD. Accounting may change the subsession identifiers to indicate such subsessions. However, the Session-Id value used for the initial authorization exchange MUST be used to generate a Session-Termination-Request when the session context is terminated.

When a NAS receives an indication that a user's session is being disconnected by the client, for example a Link Control Protocol Terminate-Request message, or an administrative command, it MUST issue a Session-Termination-Request to its Diameter server, so that resources maintained on the servers are freed appropriately. A NAS that receives an Abort-Session-Request MUST issue an Abort-Session-Answer if the session identified is active, and disconnect the PPP or tunnelling session. If accounting is active, an Accounting STOP_RECORD message MUST be sent upon termination of the session context.
sections.plainLanguage: When a caller connects, the access server sends one message with the call details and the credentials, and the server answers with permission or a refusal. If the answer asks for another round, they go round again. Once the session is running, the server can ask for it to be checked again, and when the call ends the access server tells the server so that resources are released.

sections.title: The Diameter NAS Application Messages
sections.content:
The command codes that MUST be supported by all implementations conforming to this specification are AA-Request and AA-Answer with code 265, Re-Auth-Request and Re-Auth-Answer with code 258, Session-Termination-Request and Session-Termination-Answer with code 275, Abort-Session-Request and Abort-Session-Answer with code 274, and Accounting-Request and Accounting-Answer with code 271. The request and answer of a pair share the same code and are told apart by the R bit in the Command Flags field.

The AA-Request requests authentication and/or authorization for a given NAS user, and the type of request is identified through the Auth-Request-Type attribute, for which the recommended value in most situations is AUTHORIZE_AUTHENTICATE. If authentication is requested, the User-Name attribute SHOULD be present, as well as any additional authentication attributes that carry the password information. A request for authorization SHOULD only include the information from which the authorization will be performed, such as the User-Name, Called-Station-Id or Calling-Station-Id attributes. All requests SHOULD contain attributes uniquely identifying the source of the call, such as Origin-Host and NAS-Port. It is possible for a single session to be authorized first and then for an authentication request to follow.

An AA-Request message MAY be the result of a multi-round authentication exchange, which occurs when the AA-Answer is received with the Result-Code set to DIAMETER_MULTI_ROUND_AUTH. A subsequent request SHOULD be sent with the User-Password attribute holding the user's response to the prompt, and MUST include any State attributes that were present in the answer.

The AA-Answer is sent in response to the AA-Request. If authorization was requested, a successful response includes the authorization attributes appropriate for the service being provided. For authentication exchanges needing more than one round trip, the server MUST set the Result-Code to DIAMETER_MULTI_ROUND_AUTH, and such an answer MAY include one or more Reply-Message attributes and zero or one State attributes. If the Reply-Message attribute was present, the NAS SHOULD send the text to the user's client to display, instructing the client to prompt the user for a response, for example through PAP. If it is impossible to deliver the text prompt to the user, the NAS client MUST treat the answer as an error and deny access.

The Re-Auth-Answer MUST carry a Result-Code attribute indicating the disposition of the request, and a successful transaction MUST be followed by an AA-Request. The Accounting-Request is sent by the NAS to report its session information to a target server downstream, and the Acct-Application-Id attribute MUST be present. The AVPs listed in the Diameter Base protocol MUST be assumed to be present as appropriate, and the NAS service-specific accounting attributes SHOULD be present as described in the accounting section of the RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: There are five pairs of messages: asking for access, asking again, ending the session, aborting the session, and reporting usage. Each pair has a number of its own. A reply can ask the caller for more information, in which case the access server passes that prompt on to the person.

sections.title: The NAS Application Attributes
sections.content:
The attributes used in these messages fall into groups. The session identification group describes the call itself: the NAS-Port attribute, with code 5 and type Unsigned32, holds the physical or virtual port number of the NAS that authenticates the user, where port means a service connection rather than an IP protocol identifier. The NAS-Port-Id attribute identifies the port, and the NAS-Port-Type attribute, with code 61 and type Enumerated, holds the type of port on which the NAS is authenticating the user, and SHOULD be present if the NAS uses the same port number ranges for different service types concurrently. The Called-Station-Id attribute, with code 30 and type UTF8String, holds a 7-bit US-ASCII string describing the Layer 2 address the user contacted, which for dial-up access can be a phone number obtained from the Dialed Number Identification Service, and may be different from the number the call came in on. The Calling-Station-Id attribute describes the other end. The Connect-Info and Originating-Line-Info attributes carry further call information, and the Reply-Message attribute carries text to show to the user.

The authentication group carries the credentials. The User-Password attribute, with code 2 and type OctetString, contains the password of the user to be authenticated or the user's input in a multi-round authentication exchange. Password-Retry tells the user how many attempts remain, and Prompt carries the text of the prompt to display. The CHAP-Auth attribute and its companions CHAP-Algorithm, CHAP-Ident, CHAP-Response and CHAP-Challenge carry a CHAP exchange, and the ARAP attributes carry the AppleTalk Remote Access Protocol equivalents.

The authorization group says what the user may do. The Service-Type attribute, with code 6 and type Enumerated, holds the type of service the user has requested or to be provided. Callback-Number and Callback-Id give a number to call back on, Idle-Timeout says how long an idle session may last, Port-Limit limits how many sessions the NAS may provide, and NAS-Filter-Rule, Filter-Id and QoS-Filter-Rule give the rules that apply. The Configuration-Token attribute lets the server pass a token back to the NAS for it to echo in a later request. The Framed Access attributes describe how a framed session should be set up, including Framed-Protocol, Framed-Routing, Framed-MTU and Framed-Compression, the IP access attributes such as Framed-IP-Address, Framed-IP-Netmask, Framed-Route, Framed-Pool and the IPv6 equivalents, IPX access attributes, and AppleTalk attributes. The Non-Framed Access attributes include Login-IP-Host, Login-IPv6-Host, Login-Service, the TCP service attributes such as Login-TCP-Port, and the LAT service attributes.

The tunnelling group describes a compulsory tunnel service. The Tunneling attribute, with code 401 and type Grouped, carries the Tunnel-Type, Tunnel-Medium-Type, Tunnel-Client-Endpoint, Tunnel-Server-Endpoint, Tunnel-Password, Tunnel-Private-Group-Id, Tunnel-Assignment-Id, Tunnel-Preference, Tunnel-Client-Auth-Id and Tunnel-Server-Auth-Id attributes. The client and server endpoint attributes, together with the Session-Id, give a globally unique way to identify a tunnel for accounting and auditing purposes.

The accounting group reports usage. Accounting-Input-Octets, Accounting-Output-Octets, Accounting-Input-Packets and Accounting-Output-Packets give the volumes, Acct-Session-Time, with code 46 and type Unsigned32, gives the length of the current session in seconds and can only be present in accounting requests with an Accounting-Record-Type of INTERIM_RECORD or STOP_RECORD, Acct-Authentic, with code 45 and type Enumerated, says how the user was authenticated, Accounting-Auth-Method names the method, Acct-Delay-Time records how long the server took, and Acct-Link-Count counts the links in a multilink session. The Acct-Tunnel-Connection and Acct-Tunnel-Packets-Lost attributes report on the tunnel.
sections.plainLanguage: The attributes fall into five piles: what call this is, the credentials, what the user is allowed, the tunnel if there is one, and the usage figures. Several of them are carried over from the older RADIUS attributes, with the same numbers, so that existing systems can be adapted.

sections.title: Which Attributes May Appear Where
sections.content:
The RFC provides tables that list the attributes used by NAS applications and specify in which Diameter messages they may or may not be present. Messages and attributes defined in the Diameter Base protocol are not described in the document, and attributes that can only be present within a grouped attribute are not represented in the tables. The tables use four symbols: 0 means the attribute MUST NOT be present in the message; 0+ means zero or more instances of the attribute MAY be present; 0-1 means zero or one instance of the attribute MAY be present; and 1 means exactly one instance of the attribute MUST be present in the message.

One table covers the AA-Request and AA-Answer messages and is limited to the command codes defined in this specification, listing each attribute against the two messages. Further tables cover the accounting attributes, split into framed access accounting and non-framed access accounting, because the two kinds of access service report different things.
sections.plainLanguage: For each pair of messages, a table says which fields are forbidden, which are optional, which may be repeated and which must be there exactly once. That is what lets two implementations written from this document interoperate.

sections.title: Unicode Considerations
sections.content:
A number of the attributes in this RFC use the UTF8String type of the Diameter Base protocol. Differences in Unicode input processing can result in the same Unicode input characters generating different UTF-8 strings that fail to match when compared for equality, which can cause interoperability problems between a network access server and a Diameter server when a UTF-8 string entered locally is compared with one received over Diameter. Many of the uses of UTF8String in this RFC are limited to the 7-bit US-ASCII-compatible subset of UTF-8, where this class of comparison problem does not arise.

Careful preparation of Unicode strings can increase the likelihood that string comparison will work in ways that make sense for typical users throughout the world, and RFC 3454 is given as an example of a framework for such preparation. The application has already been deployed with use of Unicode in accordance with RFC 4005, which does not require Unicode string preparation, so additional requirements for preparation in this RFC would not be backwards compatible with existing usage.

The Diameter server and the network access servers it serves can be assumed to be under common administrative control, and all of the UTF-8 strings involved are part of the configuration of these servers. Administrative interfaces SHOULD therefore accept direct UTF-8 input of all configuration strings for attributes that allow Unicode characters beyond the 7-bit US-ASCII-compatible subset, and the RFC sets out the resulting guidance for such interfaces.
sections.plainLanguage: Two programs can write the same visible characters in UTF-8 in different byte sequences, and then fail to recognise each other's strings. The RFC notes the problem, and points at a standard for preparing text so that it happens less often.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security considerations for the Diameter protocol itself are discussed in the base protocol specification, and use of this application MUST take into account the security issues and requirements of that base protocol.

This document does not contain a security protocol, but it does discuss how the PPP authentication protocols can be carried within Diameter. The use of PAP SHOULD be discouraged, as it exposes users' passwords to possibly untrusted entities, although PAP is also frequently used with one-time passwords, which do not expose a security risk. The document also describes how CHAP can be carried within Diameter, which is required for RADIUS backward compatibility, and notes that CHAP as used in a RADIUS environment facilitates authentication replay attacks. The use of the EAP authentication protocols can offer better security, given a method suitable for the circumstances.

Depending on the value of the Auth-Request-Type attribute, the Diameter protocol allows authorization-only requests that carry no authentication information from the client. This capability goes beyond the Call Check capability of RADIUS, in that no access decision is requested. As a result, a new session cannot be started as a result of a response to an authorization-only request without introducing a significant security vulnerability.

Diameter attributes often contain security-sensitive data, for example user passwords, location data, network addresses and cryptographic keys. With the exception of the Configuration-Token, QoS-Filter-Rule and Tunneling attributes, all of the attributes defined in this document are considered to be security-sensitive. Diameter messages containing any such attributes MUST only be sent protected by mutually authenticated TLS or IPsec, and MUST NOT be sent via intermediate nodes unless there is end-to-end security between the originator and the recipient, or the originator has locally trusted configuration indicating that end-to-end security is not needed. For example, end-to-end security may not be required where an intermediary node is known to be operated as part of the same administrative domain as the endpoints, so that compromising the intermediary would imply a high probability of being able to compromise the endpoints too. No end-to-end security mechanism is specified in this document.
sections.plainLanguage: Most of these attributes carry passwords, addresses or keys, so they must travel over an encrypted and mutually authenticated link, and must not be handed to an intermediate server unless that server is trusted as much as the two ends.

viz.caption: THE COMMAND CODES DEFINED BY RFC 7155

items.label: AAR / AAA
items.desc: AA-Request and AA-Answer: ask for authentication and authorization, and get the answer.

items.label: RAR / RAA
items.desc: Re-Auth-Request and Re-Auth-Answer: the server asks for the session to be checked again.

items.label: STR / STA
items.desc: Session-Termination-Request and Answer: the access server reports that the session has ended.

items.label: ASR / ASA
items.desc: Abort-Session-Request and Answer: the server tells the access server to disconnect the session.

items.label: ACR / ACA
items.desc: Accounting-Request and Answer: the access server reports what the session used.

viz.caption: ILLUSTRATIVE: THE EXCHANGE FROM A CALL ARRIVING TO THE SESSION ENDING

messages.label: AA-Request with the call details and the user's credentials
AA-Answer with authorization attributes, or DIAMETER_MULTI_ROUND_AUTH for another round
Re-Auth-Request when the authorization lifetime runs out

viz.caption: SOME OF THE ATTRIBUTES DEFINED IN RFC 7155

cells: The physical or virtual port number on which the NAS authenticates the user
The user's password, or the user's answer in a multi-round exchange
The type of service the user has requested or is to be provided
The type of port on which the NAS is authenticating the user
The Layer 2 address the user contacted, such as a dialled number
The framing to be used for framed access
The details of a compulsory tunnel service
The length of the current session in seconds

items.title: Session identification
items.text: Which call this is: the port, the numbers dialled and calling, and the connection details.

items.title: Authentication
items.text: The credentials: the password, the CHAP exchange, the ARAP exchange, and the prompts shown to the user.

items.title: Authorization
items.text: What the user may do: the service type, timeouts, port limits, filters, and the framed, non-framed and tunnelling settings.

items.title: Tunnelling
items.text: The tunnel: its type, medium, endpoints, password, private group, assignment and preference.

items.title: Accounting
items.text: The usage: octets and packets in and out, session time, how the user authenticated, delay and link counts.
